cards.text: Last time, King Hezekiah of Judah got the house of the LORD cleaned out and running again. Now he sends word throughout all Israel and Judah, and he even writes letters to Ephraim and Manasseh, inviting them all to keep the Passover of the LORD. Friend, this man is inviting the WHOLE country, and I get nervous inviting over one baker.

cards.question: Hezekiah is inviting everybody to keep the Passover. Where does he want them to come?

answers.text: The house of the LORD in Jerusalem

cards.text: One problem. The Passover has a regular time, and this year they missed it.

cards.question: Since they missed the regular time, the king, his officials and the whole assembly in Jerusalem decide to keep the Passover in the ___ month.
Why couldn't Judah keep the Passover at the regular time?

answers.text: Not enough priests had consecrated themselves
The temple doors were still locked up
The king was away fighting a war

cards.question: The plan to keep the Passover in the second month pleases the king and the whole assembly.

cards.text: So they make it official: a proclamation goes all through Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, calling the people to Jerusalem for the Passover. It hadn't been kept in great numbers the way it was written.
The couriers head out across Israel and Judah carrying letters from the king and his officials. No group chat, no email, friend, just feet, and I BET those feet hurt.

cards.question: The king's letter calls the children of Israel to return to the LORD, so that He may return to them.
The king's letter speaks to the people who remain, the ones who escaped the grasp of the kings of ___.

cards.text: Then the letter gets honest. Don't be like your fathers and brothers who were unfaithful to the LORD, and don't stiffen your necks the way they did.

cards.question: Instead of stiffening their necks, what does the king's letter tell the people to do?

answers.text: Submit to the LORD and come to His sanctuary
Build an altar to the LORD in their own town
Wait at home until a prophet comes to them

cards.question: The king's letter says that even if the people return to the LORD, their captured brothers and sons are gone for good.
The king's letter promises the LORD won't turn His face away if they come back. Why can they count on that?

answers.text: He owes their fathers a debt

cards.text: So the couriers go city to city through Ephraim and Manasseh, all the way to Zebulun. Picture walking ALL that way to hand somebody an invitation from the king himself.

cards.question: How do the people in Ephraim, Manasseh and Zebulun treat the king's couriers? They ___ and ___ them.
Some people from Asher, Manasseh and Zebulun humble themselves and come to Jerusalem.

cards.text: Mocked up north, but now look at Judah. The power of God is on the people there.

cards.question: What does the power of God give the people of Judah?

answers.text: One heart to obey the king's command
Gold to fill the house of the LORD

cards.text: All that mocking didn't stop a thing: in the second month, a VERY great assembly gathers in Jerusalem for the Feast of Unleavened Bread. But first, some cleaning.

cards.question: Before the feast, what does the great crowd in Jerusalem clear out of the city?

answers.text: The altars and the incense altars
The foreign merchants and their stalls
The old king's statues and thrones

cards.question: The crowd throws those altars out of Jerusalem and into the ___ Valley.

cards.text: On the fourteenth day of the second month, they slaughter the Passover lamb. Then something hits the priests and Levites.

cards.question: Not enough priests had consecrated themselves for the regular Passover time. Now that the Passover lamb is slaughtered, how do the priests and Levites feel?

cards.text: So they consecrate themselves, bring burnt offerings, and stand at their posts by the Law of Moses the man of God. The Levites hand the blood to the priests, and the priests splatter it.
Problem: many in the crowd hadn't consecrated themselves. So the Levites slaughter the Passover lambs for every unclean person, like one coworker covering EVERYBODY'S shift at once.

cards.question: Many people from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar and Zebulun hadn't purified themselves, so they sit out the Passover meal.

cards.text: Nope. They ate the Passover anyway, contrary to what was written, and now the king has a situation on his hands.

cards.question: Many people ate the Passover without purifying themselves. What does King Hezekiah do?
Hezekiah says, "May the LORD, who is good, provide atonement for everyone" who does what?

answers.text: Sets his heart on seeking God

cards.question: After Hezekiah intercedes, the LORD hears him and heals the people.

cards.text: The people are healed, and now the Feast of Unleavened Bread runs seven days with great joy, the Levites and priests praising the LORD day after day with LOUD instruments. After years of quiet in a junk drawer, friend, LOUD is my favorite kind of music.

cards.question: What does King Hezekiah do for the Levites who serve skillfully before the LORD?

cards.text: For seven days they eat their assigned portion, sacrifice peace offerings and give thanks to the LORD, the God of their fathers. Then the whole assembly makes a decision.

cards.question: Seven days of joy isn't enough. The whole assembly agrees to observe ___ more days.

cards.text: Hezekiah gives a thousand bulls and seven thousand sheep, the officials give a thousand bulls and TEN THOUSAND sheep, and a great number of priests consecrate themselves. Friend, I used to get nervous lending out a rolling pin.

cards.question: Only the people of Judah get to rejoice, and the foreigners are left out.

cards.text: So there's great rejoicing in Jerusalem. Nothing like it in a long, LONG time.

cards.question: Nothing like this had happened in Jerusalem since the days of ___ son of David king of Israel.
To close out the feast, the priests and Levites stand to bless the people. What happens to their prayer?

answers.text: It reaches God's holy dwelling in heaven
The king has it written in his records
The people repeat it all through the night

cards.text: And that's where we pause, friend. The oven's still warm on Hezekiah's story, and it is NOT done baking.

findings.problem: The card opens with a Bible fact from the previous passage: 'Last time, King Hezekiah of Judah got the house of the LORD cleaned out and running again' (2 Chronicles 29). The card cites only 2 Chronicles 30:1, so that fact has no reference.

rule.text: Every Bible fact he states carries its reference.

findings.problem: The card cites 2 Chronicles 30:2-3, but it only tells verse 3: they couldn't keep the Passover at the regular time. Verse 2's decision to use the second month isn't told on this card. Card 4 asks about it, so the citation should be 2 Chronicles 30:3.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: Both right answers (scorn, mock) are negative and all three wrong answers (thank, follow, welcome) are positive. A baker who guesses the reaction was negative gets both blanks without knowing the verse, so the right answers stand out by tone.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The two right answers, scorn and mock, can be swapped ('They mock and scorn them') without changing the meaning, but the JSON ties scorn to blank 1 and mock to blank 2. A baker who puts them in the other order could argue they're right.
findings.question: When the two right words in a two-blank card can be swapped without changing the meaning, should either order count as right, or should two-blank cards avoid interchangeable words?

findings.problem: The card's joke ('Picture walking ALL that way…') repeats the joke on card 8 ('just feet, and I BET those feet hurt') with no new angle. It reads like a nice dad being pleasant, not a laugh.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: 'All that mocking didn't stop a thing' stretches the text and states a connection it doesn't give. Verses 10-11 say the people scorned and mocked the couriers and only some came, so the mocking did keep many away.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: 'The old king's statues and thrones' isn't a real detail from the Bible. This is a which-thing question, so its wrong answers must be real Bible details.

rule.text: For who, which thing and where questions, wrong answers are real details from somewhere in the Bible, like Joppa when the right answer is Tarshish.

findings.problem: The question ties the shame to a cause: 'Not enough priests had consecrated themselves for the regular Passover time. Now that the Passover lamb is slaughtered, how do the priests and Levites feel?' Verse 15 only says the priests and Levites were ashamed. It doesn't say why.

rule.text: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: The story card has four things happening: they consecrate themselves, bring burnt offerings, stand at their posts by the Law of Moses, and handle the blood.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The card quotes the start of Hezekiah's line, 'May the LORD, who is good, provide atonement for everyone', and asks 'who does what?' That asks the baker to finish the line with the words that come next in verse 19.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: Stop 2 has almost no humor. Apart from the coworker comparison on card 7, every story card is plain retelling ('now the king has a situation on his hands'). The stop reads pleasant, not laugh-out-loud funny.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.

findings.problem: 'Seven days of joy isn't enough' adds a reason for the extra week. Verse 23 only says the whole assembly agreed to observe seven more days.

rule.text: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: The joke 'I used to get nervous lending out a rolling pin' invents a new past habit from his time in the Millers' kitchen. It doesn't fit a stamper who sat on the counter. Jokes may make up small moments around his bakery, but not new backstory.

rule.text: He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.
